6000:
Michael Di Salvo wrote:
>>
>>
1) Bally flash multi-cart
>>

I think that everyone likes this idea the moment that it is mentioned.  Modern technology and old technology mated together to make the "ultimate" cartridge.

>>
Anybody thought about making this type of multi-cart before?
>>

Discussion of this idea has come up before, to a limited extent.  As you've already suggested, the Bally Astrocade is limited in the cartridge area, and most expansion would have to occur through the expansion port.  I've been learning enough about electronics to get myself in trouble... but not enough to design anything (well, not anything neat-- like a multicart).  Here are my thoughts:

1) The only SERIOUS previous discussion of this was about an expansion (not a cartridge) that would work through the expansion port in very much the same fashion as described (but with no menu).  It would connect to a computer via USB.  Programs would be downloaded to it and played.  I don't think that this matches exactly with what Michael is talking about though, which is a multicart that can be updated via USB.

2) I don't think that the Astrocade's CPU can do anything in the cartridge port except read.  I think for this reason that any USB multicart would require it's own CPU (even a simple and inexpensive PIC chip would probably do fine) so that it can communicate with the PC via the USB cable.  

3) The Astrocade's cartridge area is limited to 8K.  There has NEVER been an Astrocade cartridge that uses any bank-switching techniques.  However, I don't think that there is any reason that a bankswitched cartridge can't be made.  The first 8K could hold a menu that would access the rest of RAM and switch-out with another 8K game.  Remember, this is all theory here.  Can someone please get into the nitty-gritty of how this might work?

4) The Astrocade has limited power.  An expansion that has several chips in it might require an external power supply-- i.e. wall wart.

>>
I know "this can't be done" so I've heard but all those flash carts use them.
>>

I don't recall anyone ever saying this couldn't be done.  It CAN be done.  It just requires many things to come together at once.

The easiest method for a USB device would be through the expansion port.  The Lil' White Ram expansion goes quite a bit in that direction.  You can load cartridges into it via the AstroBASIC input (using the conversion program that Lance wrote-- which I still have not tried).  Once the data is in the Lil' Blue Ram, a switch can be thrown.  When the Astrocade is reset, the game starts just as if it were a cartridge.  If the Lil' White Ram loaded games via the USB port, then it would be most of the way there.  Still, it would only hold one game at a time, plus there is no menu.

A menu-driven multicart could be created via the cartridge port, but it would require more circuitry, and, like I said, it's own CPU.  This would probably be pretty expensive.

Creation of this menu-driven multicart would require expertise in several areas:

1) Z-80 Programming (Assembly) - This would be needed to create, at the least, the menu.  If the expansion port were used, then the Z-80 would control communication (via USB) with the PC as well.

2) PC Programming (C++) - A program on the PC side would need to control the communication with the multicart.

3) PIC Programming (C or Assembly) - The multicart, not having access to the the Z-80 CPU, would require its own  CPU to be able to communicate with the PC.

4) Hardware Design - The multicart or expansion device would have to designed.

5) PCB Design - This is NOT the same as hardware design.  For a complicated device, as has been discussed, a PCB would have to be designed.  There could be no wire-wrapping (old school) or homemade PCB (via a laser printer) as these would require WAY too much time to make each multicart.

As can be seen, for such a multicart to come together, there would have to be a REALLY talented person, or small group of talented people.  Don't lose hope though.  These people DO exist, as can be seen by their creations for just about all the other classic systems that have a USB-type multicart.  This device that we're discussing just would take a person with a REAL enthusiasm for the Astrocade.  A person that knows not to expect more than, at most, a few dozen sales.

Adam

6001:
Re: Adams last post:

If I recall the 'Can't be done' was referring to using address lines or writing to the cart to make the bank switch happen.

I had thought that a cable from either the expansion port or a joystick port could facilitate this, but that would be .... messy.

If I had the where with all to design a menu driven USB flash multicart, I would make it a 2 piece deal.

Part 1 would be the cart. It would be a standard cart (possabily with audio interface for those programs)

The program on it would be a menu generator that looked at part 2 for the list of programs and addresses/banks they were in.

Once a selection was made, the cart would cause part 2 to switch banks and execute/reset the program there.

Part 2 obviously would be the expansion port flashRam, usb interface.

Weather this would actually work effectively I don't know.

Just my thoughts on the subject.

I have created a new documentation area on Ballyalley.com for the Ward Shrake Multicart.  Most of these documents are new, although a few have been moved here from the multicart picture area.  Ward has given his blessing to use this information to create other multicarts as long as, he says, "folks credit my work, if they use all of or part of the design" (see the release letter below for additional information about this).  Here is the information now in this area:

1)  Multicart 7432 Truth Table (Original) - Notes from September 27, 2001.

2)  Multicart 7432 Truth Table (Simplified) - Notes from September 27, 2001.

3)  Multicart 7432 Visualization Aide - Notes on how the 7432 (Quad 2-Input OR Gate) works with the dipswitches on the multicart. Notes from September 27, 2001.

4)  Multicart Board Revision Notes - Multicart revision notes from December 18, 2001.

5)  Multicart DipSwitch Setting - DIP Switch Settings for the "Bally Astrocade" Multicart version 1.3a (that's the last version of the ROM). These documents should be considered the instructions for the cartridge. This zipped download
includes two Word Documents, two PDF documents and a text document; use the pdf documents, not the Word documents (which are included in case any changes need to be made).  Two documents are the same information sorted into two different ways: alphabetically and alphabetically sorted by extra RAM needed or not. The last document shows which dipswitch settings are still available.

6)  Multicart FAQ - This text answers people's questions about the Astrocade and Arcadia multicarts that Ward Shrake created. Document date is January 25, 2002.

7)  Multicart FAQ (Update) - This FAQ covers Ward Shrakes "Bally Astrocade" and "Emerson Arcadia 2001" multicarts.  Ward reaffirms that no more Astrocade multicarts will be sold to the public. Document date is April 16, 2008.

8)  Multicart Jumper Assembly Steps and Tips - Multicart jumper assembly steps and tips. Including wire color and length, as well as much more detailed final jumper wire routing. Notes from December 13, 2002.

9)  Multicart Jumper-Wire Template - An index card with short notes on how to set-up the jumper wires. This was written in December 2002.

10) Astrocade Multicart - Photo Mask (Part 1)

11) Astrocade Multicart - Photo Mask (Part 2)

12) Ward Shrake's Release Letter - Ward Shrake gave permission on January 3, 2008 to use his documentation to create another multicart-- one that could be identical to his own.  This letter is written to Adam Trionfo, the man who has assembled the Ballyalley.com website.

The following is the Multicart release letter that Ward Shrake sent to me back in early January.

Adam:

I'm not sure what to call the attached, in terms of legalisms or whatever -- either "Released into the Public Domain" or "I won't complain if other folks make transparencies from this artwork, and then etch new Bally multi-carts" ... or what? In any case, I'm sending all this zipped stuff to you, for you to put on your web site. (As we had briefly discussed, before.)

To make it clear that I'm not sticking 100% to the letter of whatever, I ran "strike-through" lines through the portions of the photo mask artwork that once had a copyright message.

I guess my only concern is having folks credit my work, if they use all of part of the design. If they do that, I can't imagine any other concerns I'd have? A lot of things got released as an "I don't mind if you use this (old work someone had done)" sort of thing. So ... "me too".

I realize some questions from collectors or electronically-inclined folks may be inevitable. I'll try to answer them, later, as best I can ... but for now, just tell your readers that any notes I had, which once equated to (one-man) "factory" instructions, boiled down to four things:

(1.)  Experience and personal memory. The multi-carts were all being done in batches, one after another. So ... "I'll remember." (Yeah, sure! Then? Yes. Now ... not necessarily!) I had to re-figure some details out, via studying the stuff I'm sending you now ... and via some stuff I didn't send, which I still have PC backups of. (Mostly, other revisions to the mask artwork.)

(2.)  Whenever I didn't remember some detail or other, I'd get out my "made for Ward" multi-cart(s). I remember using that a lot, for things like remembering the exact routing "map" -- and it was pretty picky: not much space inside that cartridge shell! -- of the jumper wires, or just as a general purpose "copy this" prototype, for things like where to solder each resistor. I had two such carts: the first one ever made (which you now own: the "hole in case" one) and a personal one that I sold to B.G.'s wife at around Christmas 2004. My memory of it was that the personal one would have been more relevant as a template / prototype ... the one you have (#00) that used to be mine, had enough subtle changes to be a bit limiting, as time went on. The one B.G. has (#13) was at least a revision B board; and therefore closer if not exactly like the real thing. (I didn't track board revisions / cart ... I don't think, anyway?)

(3.)  The attached "jumpers.txt" file was the closest thing I ever had, to written assembly documentation. I don't recall absolutely for sure (and it hardly matters) but I may have had a hand-scribbled "first draft" of that text (which I would have thrown out, upon typing it all in: to avoid confusion on which version superceded which). The text got revised a bit, as time went on: mostly because I started routing jumpers a little different. (Later than the big scans I'm sending, of cart #69. That seems to be a revision B board design; before I ran out of two of the colors of wire I had used, for carts previous to that. Reading the jumpers.txt again, today, and comparing it to the scans of cart #69, some of the text is almost a "huh?" deal ... the two sources don't seem to match, 100% ... so I must have been using one of the actual boards as a "copy this" prototype, at about that time. Presumably, after having to desolder the EPROM chip, to upgrade it for some new addition or other? That's my current memory.

(4.)  I'm not in any hurry to go back and re-read that old multi-cart FAQ! ... especially given my weariness / attitude, towards the end of the production run! ... but I vaguely recall using it at times, to track things like dates or minor revisions to procedures; as I made my multi's. Kind of a quick "Oh, yeah" thing ... so I could get back to inhaling etching / soldering fumes.


Other assorted notes about the "history" of the 43 multi-carts I made for the Astrocade:
 

I don't recall exactly why multi-cart #69 was picked, for scanning in. Maybe it was just time for me to get more "organizee" on my little card table "assembly line"? I seem to remember thinking it'd be easier if I had a big blow-up on a screen, to look sideways at, as I soldered?

Related to that, is this: I went through my old hard drive backups, and came up with three slight revisions to the PC board's photo mask artwork. I didn't label the first revision, per se; and I didn't do much to distinguish the second from the first, as far as labeling it differently. (If anyone's really Wildly Jones-ing for such info, I can study the differences and come up a few words and pics?) By the time I got around to making revision "C," I felt it was time to put that info onto the PC board itself, as I etched each board. Those three revisions were what made up the 43 multi-carts that I made and sold around 2000/1 to 2003. I doubt many of the Revision A boards got made; most were probably Revision B boards; and a relatively small amount of Revision C boards, towards the last batches. (A-to-B was, I think, an "oops" deal in terms of electronics; which I probably corrected with a cutter in a Dremel tool, rather than have to waste all that work. The change from B-to-C, as I recall it now, was minor stuff that would just make it easier for me to assemble the boards by hand: longer solder pads, etc.)

The "Revision D" photo masks I'm sending to you now are essentially a slight (2008) revision to the (stable) "Revision C" artwork. I did that work tonight. I did not alter the circuit design, but I did make some changes to the text that gets etched into the board's metal surface.

To keep original owners happy, I stuck a "Reproduction --- not an original" notice on Rev. "D" -- in the hope that whatever collector value there is for the first 43 carts I made, stays intact: even if later MC's end up being made, if/when talented folks etch using the latest artwork? I see that as the best compromise I can do, to both accommodate older and newer MC users.

Initially, I couldn't remember the reason why I had two of each board, per "drawing" ... until I got out and studied my actual photo-etching transparencies. (Which I still have.) The reason behind two component "sides" plus two solder "sides" has to do with raw (uncut) PC board sizes. It was much more efficient for me to etch two of each (Bally or Emerson) multi-cart boards at once. Those two tops and two bottoms, when printed out as inkjet transparencies ("process camera," my foot! Ha! I wish, but not on my budget!) became the photo masks for the tops and bottoms of two boards-to-be, etched as if only one board; then cut into two of them. Etching pairs was much quicker / easier: a (very) little "economy of scale" going on. (When etching boards at home, you don't always get perfect results. Almost never, actually: which is one reason I drew it all with such "fat" traces. So: if one half was too messed up to use, after etching was completed, I hadn't wasted all of that etching time ... only half of it.)

I have some (cheapie 110 film) photos, somewhere, of my little card table "assembly line". I'd have to find them in my travels, but they're around here somewhere: seen 'em recent-ish.

If you (or your web site's viewers) have any questions about all this, I'll do what I can to figure out / remember what I did, six or seven years ago now ... and try to answer as best I can. (But I can't / won't describe every single technical step ... that's several years of college!)

Ward Shrake

PART 1

I promissed that I'd do a review of Gambits Ulti-multi, but I began
to wonder if everyone would think that I'm biased. So I'll begin with
a disclaimer, Yes I'm biased, towards Ward Shrake's ORIGIONAL! The
reason this is, unlike Gambits (which was all Ken Lill) I DID get
involved in the creation of Wards Multicart. There were three of us
doing work for it at the time Ward, Adam, and I. All of the Basicart
programs that appeared on Wards cart came from EPROMS that I had
to "engineer" and send to him. See Bally Alley where my tutorials
reside to read about the 2x4 (and 4x2) Basicart loaders. These were
created just for Wards Multicart! The origional Basicart's used a
modified form of Astrobasic and had it all burned into a "play
instantly" cartridge using a 2764 EPROM with the program loading in
via on-board subroutine 95 (as per Leroy Flamm). This would mean that
Astrobasic would need to be copied into the multicart over a dozen
times! The loaders eliminated all that, and allowed Ward to get more
programs into a smaller EPROM. Bet you cannot guess exactly how many
times Astrobasic (modified or not) appears in Wards Multicart.
Besides the Basicarts, there were the "prototype" game carts to get
to Ward and Adam to be included also. Although the final work was all
Wards. Besides Adam, (and perhaps Jamie) I was the only other person
to recieve one without the $100.00 price tag (for the programs I
contributed). In the end, the genuine Ward Shrake Multicart will
always be the "collectors choice" as the others are "copycats" by 
comparison. Note: the others may have value 35 years from now, but my
bet is still on the origional first Bally-Astrocade Multicart for a
good return, if there is to be anything at all!!

There are now Four different Multicarts for our system (not counting
the numerious variations) that I'm aware of and if someone in the
group knows of yet another besides:

Ward Shrake
CPUWIZ
Retrokids
Gambits

Please, let's hear about it. Each has a "unique" listing of programs.
Meaning that each one has something that the others don't. They all
appear to have all of the released games from Bally, Astrovision,
Astrocade, and the 3rd party venders that made anything "back in the
day". The differences begin with the unfinished prototypes and
the "Basicarts". No single cartridge has just "EVERYTHING" as the
creaters of such felt it a waste to repeat some programs, or include
redundencies such as the Astrobasic and Blue Ram Basic versions of
the same games. Other differences appear with construction. I don't
as of this writing have access to a Retrokids Multicart to see what
it looks like inside, but as for the others, Ward Shrake's has the
most, as he used his space to the greatest effenciency, Gambits is
next (with more to say about this) and CPUWIZ wastes the most space.
Ward Shrake has a "hommade" board inside his, Gambits uses a
professionally made board, and CPUWIZ uses an old Bally Cart board
and a "perf" board (probabily from Radio Shack) hacked together by
hand. CPUWIZ however, has (in this persons opinion) the best looking
label.

Back in 1987 I sent out a Flier where I began a critical review of
some of my own wares. (It too is on Bally Alley) I began it by
quoting an old saying that goes "you get what you pay for, and
sometimes less!" Think about it, then let's hear a feedback comment
or two. I WILL continue this (as there is something developing here)
but this won't be complete without the other Multicart(s) being
represented.

Until then, if you play games using a Multicart with Lil' White Ram,
use Gambits (first choice) or Ward Shrake's (second choice).

Mike W.

I suddenly remembered that I meant to reply to this and never did.  Part of it is that the Astrocade driver wasn't updated for a long time, then got switched over to the MAME implementation, which caused some bugs during the transition.  Also, Richard's been testing some of the more obscure behavior such as interrupt timings.

But in general, you will find a lot of bugs popping up in MESS, because it's constantly in flux, and there are so many systems that they don't always get tested thoroughly when something changes.  A release is almost just a snapshot of where the code repository happens to be at that moment.  Anyone who's really interested in MESS should set up a compile environment for the SVN code.  That way they can pick up a bug fix as soon as it's committed.  And of course, testers are always wanted.

I created a new section called "Astrocade, Inc. Marketing Materials" on Ballyalley.com.  I added fourteen documents  to this area.  Paul Thacker did the scanning.  There is a LOT here, so check it out and let us know what you think.  Here is what has been added:

1)  Astrocade, Inc. File Folder - File folder that Astrocade, Inc. used to distribute varying documentation.

2)  Astrocade, Inc. Price Listing (Direct) - A 1982 direct price listing. Mentions Zgrass-100 Computer with Keyboard ($419, $599 Retail).

3)  Astrocade, Inc. Price Listing (Distributor) - A 1982 distributor price listing. Mentions Zgrass-100 Computer with Keyboard ($340, $599 Retail).

4)  Astrocade: The Professional Arcade" 1982 Consumer Ad Campaign - Magazine and TV "blitz" ad campaign. Quite an impressive line-up. This says that commercials would be placed during forty-eight different TV shows and print ads in sixteen different magazines. Check out where Astrocade, Inc. planned to put ads in 1982.

5)  Astrocade: The Professional Arcade, Expandable Computer System - Small promotional flyer advertising the games for the Astrocade. There are many color screenshots as well as pictures of ten upcoming releases (four of which never came out). There is quite a bit of information packed into these few pages.

6)  Astrocade (TM) Video Game by Astrocade, Inc. - Promotional high-quality grayscale photo titled "Astrocade (TM) Video Game by Astrocade, Inc." This photo features the Astrocade with five games (Football, Grand Prix / Demolition Derby, Space Fortress, Astro Battle and Galactic Invasion).

7)  Bally Professional Arcade Plus (First Version) - This is a generic ad for dealers to use. There are no screenshots of built-in games, but the ad does have eight other screenshots. The 2000-BAUD version of BASIC included with this package is called "Bally BASIC." This ad mentions the soon-to-come Zgrass-32 expansion keyboard. Price is 299.55.

8)  Bally Professional Arcade Plus (Second Version) - This is a generic ad for dealers to use. There are screenshots of the three built-in games (and the calculator) and eight other screenshots. The 2000-BAUD version of BASIC included with this package is called "Bally BASIC." This ad does NOT mention the Zgrass-32 expansion keyboard. Price is 299.55.

9)  Bally Professional Arcade Plus (Third Version) - This is a generic ad for dealers to use. There are screenshots of the three built-in games (and the calculator). The 2000-BAUD version of BASIC included with this package is called "Astrocade BASIC." This ad does NOT mention the Zgrass-32 expansion keyboard. Price is not specified.

10) Cooperative Advertising Program Manual - This manual covers: General Policy, Method of Fund Accrual, Claiming Submittal, Method of Payment, Eligible Advertising Media, Displays and Other POP Material.

11) "Here's What They Say..." - Quotes from 1982 about the Astrocade from ten different magazines.

12) Order Form (Triplicate) - Astrocade, Inc. order form. Includes cartridges that were never released (i.e. Conan and Music Maker) as well as the Zgrass expansion.

13) Sales Meeting (1981) - The agenda for the Astrovision, Inc. one-and-a-half day Chicago sales meeting from March 20-21 1981.

14) Sales Meeting (1982) - The agenda for the Astrocade, Inc. half-day sales meeting on June 5 1982.

variables starting at -26486 (well into the upper half of memory) and
two-letter "variables" BC, FA, FB, FC, XR, XL, YT, YB, NT, CX, CY,

SZ (the BASIC area size function) prints out 5628 bytes and L.

Arrows  (so missing some arithmetic operators)

2000 baud  (WOW, even AB had that)

RPL  (no easy editing or self-modifying code)

OP  (no user commands)

PLAY  (the command in question)

!9000 = !7000  (TEXT area was moved ?)

128x256=HOW  (a math error later fixed?)

and 200 nested GOSUBs, not 67  (as in BB?)

I have added three prototype ROM images to Ballyalley.com.  These programs were all part of the Bob Fabris collection.  The three programs are:

1) ADS System Monitor - Author Unknown  2K (Actual program size: 1,533 bytes) - A machine language monitor program that uses an overlay. It is unknown if this program is complete. No previous mention of this program was known until the EPROM was found.  No documentation exists for this program.  This program could have really have grown to have more options, had the author desired.

2) Fawn Dungeon - Barry McCleave  2K (Actual program size: About 1,856 bytes)- An incomplete machine language game written by someone that corresponded with Bob Fabris (the editor and publisher of the Arcadian newsletter). The player in this D&D-type game can wander around a randomly created maze, but there are no monsters. This is an interesting piece of what might have become something interesting. As it stands, it is little more than a programming exercise.  No previous mention of this program was known until the EPROM was found.  As Barry McCleave mentions in a letter that he wrote to Bob Fabris, there is plenty of room for this program to grow, about six more kilobytes-- so an 8K cart would only be about 1/4 full.

3) Rainbow - Version 2 - Hanson  2K (Actual program size: 389 bytes) - A program that puts a nice 256-color display on the screen. Note that the EPROM was noted with a sticker as "Ver. 2." No earlier version of this program have been found.  This is just a short example program, and it's pretty neat that it fits snugly in about four-hundred bytes.  There was a VHS videotape that had this program running before a demo of Color BASIC, so it was presumed that the program was written in Color BASIC-- it was a surprise to discover that it was a machine language program written to run as a cartridge.

All programs can be downloaded here:

"LATEST MICROS OFFER POWER AND GRAPHICS"

     Color appears to be the rising attraction as a user-oriented

voice synthesizer, and is totally oriented toward color.

     The system, designed by Jeff Frederiksen, developer of the coin-op
circuitry used in Bally arcade games, says it's the only personal
computer that approaches the realism and animation capability found on
coin-operated arcade machines.  This wizardry is achieved by employing
three microprocessors, 4K of Ram, 8K of ROM (expandable to 32K), and an
optional Astro BASIC in ROM cartridge.

     The custom-designed video processor chip, operating at 7MHz, handles
all color manipulation and NTSC broadcast quality video.  The result is
a color display that rivals even expensive commercial graphics
processors.

time in video games and two at a time with Astro Basic).  The screen is
continually mapped in 4K RAM allowing for complex imagery that
approaches that found on expensive CAD graphics systems.

interfacing to hand-held controls, and is responsible for producing
music equal to that available on expensive music synthesizers.

6084:
Radio Electronics
April 1983

VIDEOGAMES column
Danny Goodman, contributing editor


"ASTROCADE'S THE INCREDIBLE WIZARD for ASTROCADE"

     Life for the ASTROCADE (formerly BALLY ARCADE) console and its
owners has not been too easy of late.  For one thing, there have always
been pretty slim pickings when it came to cartridges.  For another, the
manufacturer's (Astrocade. Inc.'s) precarious financial situation, which
has become common knowledge in these past few months, has put the future
of the machine in doubt.  However, to paraphrase Mark Twain, reports of
its death may have been greatly exaggerated.  The company, at press
time, was undergoing reorganization and is hopeful that it can continue
producing the console and even introduce some new cartridges in the near
future.

     In any event, most of the cartridges that do exist are of high
quality, owing largely to the vast graphics and sound resources of the
ASTROCADE console electronics.  One such cartridge is THE INCREDIBLE
WIZARD, Astrocade's home version of the mildly successful Midway arcade
game, THE WIZARD OF WOR.

     The game can be played by one or two persons.

     In the game, your warrior descends through many different mazes,
battling three different kinds of creatures.  The farther you get in the
game, the faster and more numerous the creatures become,  Some of the
creatures are invisible unless you're in their line of sight (when it
may be too late), so a radar screen without maze walls indicates the
approximate locations of the unseen menaces.  When all of the creatures
have been blasted by your "concentrated unified-field-disturbance rifle"
the flying Worluk appears.  You've got to shoot him before he either
runs you down or escapes through one of the side escape doors.  If you
get him, the next maze scores double point-values.  At random maze
levels, the hooded Wizard will appear, racing about like crazy, hurling
lightning bolts.  If you are good enough to shoot him, you'll experience
a fantastic light and sound show as the dungeon trembles, and your next
maze will be worth quadruple points.  At higher levels, mazes show up
that have no visable walls.  As in the arcade game, those are called
pits.

     Graphic detail is fine enough to see that your Warrior is suited up
in a helmeted space suit with a back pack.  When he shoots, the kick
from the rifle blast sets him back on his heels for a half second.

     A diverse sound package adds to the appeal of the cartridge.  The
chirp-like sound of some of the creatures, the rifle blasts hitting a
target, the disorienting sound of the trembling dungeon, and musical
interludes all help to keep things interesting.

     In many respects, including Astrocade's rather nice hand controller,
THE INCREDIBLE WIZARD is much more enjoyable than its arcade ancestor.

Chart:
Graphics   8   Good
Sound      9   Excellent
Ease of learning 7  Good
Challenge  9   Excellent
Value      9   Excellent


[Compare that to their July '83 rating of...]
CBS Video Games' WIZARD OF WOR for Atari 2600
Overall: "Excessive Flicker"
Chart:
Graphics   4   Fair
Sound      6   Good
Ease of learning 6  Good
Challenge  8   Good

6085:
Radio Electronics
September 1983

VIDEOGAMES column
Danny Goodman, contributing editor


"ROLLING YOUR OWN"

[...] For those who like to program their own games, there is another
game system - and a darn good one at that - that has been open to user
programming for years.  And you don't need assembly language or a
computer to get anywhere.  I'm talking about the unit that started out
as the Bally PROFESSIONAL ARCADE, more recently known as the ASTROCADE
(shown in figure 1 [no figure 1]).

     The system has had a long and checkered career in the volatile
videogame industry.  As we go to press, the future of AstroCade is
unsure as they attempt to extricate themselves from Chapter XI.  But
that's not what this story is about.

     As a good many of the estimated 120,000 Astrocade owners know, the
ASTROCADE, in addition to playing some of the graphically and sonically
best videogame cartridges ever, is programmable in Basic with the help
of the BASIC language/cassette-interface adapter.  In recent times, this
accessory and well prepared BASIC tutorial/reference manual has been
included as standard equipment with the unit.

     The open access to the Astrocade has caused a closely knit and loyal
following of Astrocade enthusiasts to band together in users groups and
in open exchange of information via the major news pipeline for
Astrocaders called THE ARCADIAN, a monthly newsletter published by Bob
Fabris (3626 Morrie Dr., San Jose, CA  95127).  Each issue contains
program listings and more advanced programming tips from experienced
users like Andy Guevera.

     Andy has taken his interest in the Astrocade up to the
assembly-language level (Z80 microprocessor).  But in so doing, he has
left tracks for others to follow.  He now produces a plug-in cartridge
called the MACHINE LANGUAGE MANAGER (The Bit Fiddlers, P.O.Box 11023,
San Diego, CA  92111-0010), which guides the way for novice programmers.
You'll still need to know Z80 machine language, but in the manual that
comes with the cartridge, Andy recommends some introductory books.
Machine language allows you to program faster action within the limited
built-in RAM of the Astrocade.  But there is still plenty going on in
BASIC.

     The 114-page ASTROCADE SOURCEBOOK (635 Los Alamos Ave., Livermore,
CA  94450), produced semi-annually by Richard Houser, lists practically
every one of the hundreds of third-party programs available - a large
percentage of them in Basic on cassette.  Most of these tapes have been
designed by dedicated hobbyists with a love for the capabilities of the
Astrocade system.  Every once in a while, one of these hobbyists finds a
programming specialty.

     George Moses, for example, had unlocked the secrets to the three
voice music synthesizer of the Astrocade.  His company (George Moses
Co., P.O.Box 686, Brighton, MI  48116) offers several cassettes of
straight music (Scott Joplin rags, Christmas carols, Bach and more)
playable through the console's synthesizer.  For the musically creative,
he also has a music assembler program to let you try your hand at it.

     George, by the way, produced the continuously running musical score
for one of the first third-party game cartridges for the Astrocade, a
family-oriented game called TREASURE COVE by SPECTRE SYSTEMS (Box 1741,
Dearborn, MI  48121).  Brett Bilbrey, one of the principals at SPECTRE,
was attracted to the Bally system back in 1977 (in the days of the
Fairchild CHANNEL F and dedicated ATARI videogames) because he could do
things with the BASIC cartridge that no other videogame could let him
do.  Since then, Bret and a few others have turned what was a hobby
interest into a career designing games for the Astrocade.

     With the right system, imagination, and a strong desire to master
the technical side of programming in BASIC or (preferably) machine
language, rolling your own videogames is certainly within almost
anyone's reach.

There are several Astrocade books just waiting to be written, beginning with the "enthusiasts [that] band[ed] together in users groups."  How about these ideas:

1) The Astrocade Cult Phenomenon - This book would not need to be about the technology or the games.  It would cover how people used the Astrocade, usually, with BASIC.  It would discuss how the newsletters and small user-groups formed and helped to shape the course of the system and the third-party sales.  The best book about this subject would certainly be one that talked with the people involved at the time (late seventies and early eighties), but there is enough second-source material (even if the author never ventured past Ballyalley.com!) that if someone sifted through all the documents and presented the material well, then there would be a great book.

2) History of the Astrocade - This book would require more effort to write.  It could be a history of the machine and how it ties in with the arcade systems.  I'm not just talking about how "Wizard of Wor" or "Gorf" are based on the chipset, but also how the Astrocade chipset evolved from earlier arcade cabinets by Dave Nutting.  I'd love to read interviews with hardware designers and game programmers.

3) Games - Though there are not that many cartridges, there could EASILY be a book of reviews written about all games (including tapes).  This is sort of a no-brainer.

All of these books could be combined into one book, but each of these books really does require a book of its own.  Such niche books would have to be self-published, not because of vanity, but because the audience for books like this would be extremely small.

You can bet that I'd buy the book(s)!

6126:
Mike White has asked, basically, "Why not upgrade your Astrocade with more RAM?"  Here is my reply to his question.

In the Amiga community (stay with me, I WILL tie this to the Astrocade!) in the mid-to-late nineties pressure was put on people to upgrade their machines.  This pressure was put on users from a very unusual location.  It came from the software "pirates."  The people that cracked programs got tired of people still using bog-standard Amiga 500 machines (by 1998 this computer was about ten years old-- based on the Amiga 1000, which is technology from 1985).  These crackers figured that if more people owned better machines then better software would be written for the Amiga market.  Most new games continued to work on standard machines (1MB of RAM, and required no hard drive).  However, the cracks for new games did NOT work on the standard machines anymore.  This was done on purpose in the hopes of FORCING people to upgrade.  It was a strange idea.  I doubt that it worked.

Most people blamed pirating software for the death of computers such as the Amiga and Atari ST.  The pirates though, well, they blamed companies for not making software that took advantage features of the new computers.  In fact, it was a bit of each-- though mainly it was just that the Amiga market had become so tiny that it wasn't cost effective to make programs for that line of computers anymore (and there are probably dozens of reasons for this).  A flame war would probably be started if this topic were brought up on an Amiga or Atari ST board.

It doesn't matter which computer is talked about.  Eventually that platform will stop being supported.  This has happened to even the most popular platforms.  When the Macintosh switched from the 68K CPU (the same CPU used in the Amiga and Atari ST computers) to the Power PC, the old Macs were left in the cold.  Sure, some companies supported them for a few years, but eventually that support dried up.  It's happened in the PC world too.  Try running old software on a PC.  It ain't gonna happen (unless you use emulation).

Astrocade users that used there systems as serious computers should have upgraded and got more memory.  But how many "serious" users were there?  Weren't most users casual users-- especially by about 1982 or 1983?  Most Astrocade users probably just wanted to play games on an inexpensive machine.  The problem with this RAM upgrade scheme is that it was certainly more cost effective to get a new home computer system, say one like the Atari 8-bit series or the Commodore 64.  Along with the memory you got MANY more features with a new computer.

I'm not knocking adding memory to the Astrocade.  Every person that uses an Astrocade nowadays should have extra RAM.  Everyone!  That's because anyone that still using the Astrocade today is a serious user, or at least a serious collector.  These are the exact type of people that need expanded systems.  If you're reading this then you're a serious user, so what are you waiting for?

Adam

additional RAM that the upgrades offered allowed more sophisticated
programs and more screen area to be used.  If a BASIC version of

been little reason for most users to expand their Astrocades.  It would
have taken DOZENS (maybe hundreds) of programs to be written

expanded systems before they write the software, yet the users want

timeless problem.

Footnote on "timeless problem"

The extra ram is one issue, and Extended Basic is another. One could
write a machine language program that starts from a cartridge but is
no longer limited to the 8k restraint of the cartridge slot! All one
would need to do this is a Memory Expansion! The game could be loaded
similiar to the way Quadra was, or plugged into the expansion port.

switching" circuitry even if one could figure out how (and I believe
it is possible) because of a problem built into the Arcade that I'm
working on presenting in "Multi-carts part 3". This would mean that
extended memory would be required for such a project, but not
extended basic. The problem here is how do you advertise something
like that when the buyer can't see it or try it out? Take it to shows
maybe? Up till this year that may have been the answer, but right now
no one even believes there is any working Arcades left. Even if I had
a pile of Bally War cartridges to sell at the next show, I really
doubt that I could sell more than about two! And those to collectors
(the Zip lock freezer bag crowd), not game players! This is the
real "timeless problem" as I see it. It's effected extended memory 
products since 1984 being fueled by talk of $275.00, or todays $59.95
being so much of a barracade to the purchase of an extended memory,
that readers believe that it is!
The problem with extended basic is as I said before, The Name BASIC!
Unless one actually sees otherwise one is going to believe what
Michael Prosisse "THE GAME PLAYER" said "AVOID! WATCH YOUR $$$
FOLKS!!!" The demonstrator that came with Blue Ram Basic was in
reality a stage in the development of one of the game cartridges and
was transplanted into the cartridge. It may even be possible to take
the music string out of the cartridge and use it with this
demonstrator via the play command. Then you would have everything
except the "slapstick routine" that Joe Santuli liked. (see DP guide
#6 or #7). To most "game players" it runs SLOW! TOO SLOW! But smooth!
Even Toby said it would be SLOW in his tournament, but I didn't read
him write about it not being smooth!

6162:
Mike White wrote:
>>
I DON'T recommend putting [the extra RAM] in the cartridge slot with "bank
switching" circuitry even if one could figure out how (and I believe
it is possible) because of a problem built into the Arcade that I'm
working on presenting in "Multi-carts part 3".
>>

This has me quite curious.  Many (most?) of the classic game systems have bank-
switching cartridges to get them beyond their original limitations.  For instance, by
the early nineties the bank-switching cartridges for the Commodore 64 had
reached 512K.  The first game on the Atari 2600, I THINK, to take advantage of
bank-switching was Asteroids (that was right around 1981).  Thinking back, I'm
hard pressed to think of even one system (except for REALLY obscure consoles)
that do not have bank-switched cartridges.  What would limit the Astrocade in this
area?  Of course, like any other bank-switched cartridge, the software has to be
written with bank-switching in mind.

Adam

6163:
As a sidenote on this, bank switching is a standard technique in Z80-based MSX computers, both for game cartdriges and memory expansions. Among the methods used there are the the "famous" megarom cartdriges (megarom stands for megabit rom) and memory mappers, the standard memory expansion for MSX2 and above, capable of addressing 4 megabytes of ram (16kb * 256 banks).


Ronaldo Goulart

PART 3

Well, this "article" has generated some lively discussion! But rather
than dwell on that, this part will move forward instead! I asked if
anyone could guess where the two "modified" Astro Basics resided in 
Ward Shrake's (and every other "copycat") Multi-cart. The answer was
with Candyman and Road Toad! These two programs place machine code on
the screen and then jump into Astro Basic. They cannot wait for
switches to be thrown. Try this: Select Wavemakers program tape #20
(QB2B) from any Multi-cart, and when it asks you to switch to AB,
switch to Candyman or Road Toad instead. IT WILL RUN!
Back in Part 1, I looked at the efficency of three of these Multi-
carts but didn't have the 4th at the time to look at. Retrokids Multi-
cart uses the same select convention as CPUWIZ and therefore has gaps
of 4K and 6K throughout both EEPROMs (note this). They're both
socketed as well, for easy removal with a special tool. Also, this
cart as I indicated earlier uses a professionaly made circuit board.
I happen to know that Ken had to pay $400.00 up front to engineer the
boards that he used in Gambits Multi's, I can only assume the
engineering charge on the first board was about the same here.

However, before this can continue, I must put a puzzling scenero
before this entire group by asking this:

WHAT IS YOUR ARCADE WORTH TO YOU? Sound strange? The only reason this
comes up is because as of 2008 a broken Arcade is worth the same as
one that works, especially if you tried to sell one at CCAGSHOW! I
sold an Arcade there for $120.00 to a guy that knew (at least of)
Lance Squire, and didn't live too far away. He bought the "bundle" to
get one item! I offered another unit at $55.00 to him that I was
willing to plug into my TV and let him watch for a couple hours, but
NO he didn't care about that. He wanted "the prize" that came with
the 1st one! As I said in PART 2, it was not the box, not a memory
expansion, not even a Multi-cart. What's left? He paid $120.00 for
the "bundle" to get hand controller #3 and #4! Now, to those that
claim to have "PILES" of those, you WERE sitting on a gold mine,
because knob #3 and #4 sold at a higher price than some shipping
boxes! (and FAR HIGHER than a lone Arcade was going for)! AGAIN I
say, those two items (which usually appear together as a set) are NOT
just EVERYWHERE, and the buyers at CCAGSHOW WOULD have scarfed them
up as fast as I could have provided them! But from now on I'm not so
sure, as people believe "there are no more working units left", who
needs any hand controller? (or any other device for this console for
that matter) And so I come back to the same question (considering I'm
still speaking to owners of WORKING Arcades):

WHAT IS YOUR ARCADE WORTH TO YOU, REALLY?

Let's take a look back to 1977. When the BPA was being engineered the
engineers had to cut production costs by cutting corners and NOT
putting sonething in the console that wasn't ABSOLUTELY necessary.
The unit was built to play games from PROM cartridges that resembled 
cassettes. The Add-under was planed for, and an "expansion port" was
included for this purpose (see Arcadian Vol.1 pg.21 and pay
particular attention as to how it plugs in). Also, a light pen was
allowed for, with a special jack for it (very few Arcades it seems
came with the "standard" 156mm jack, the rest had one that could only
be found on a Bally Arcade). Here I will pause to ask this of the
people that recently purchased the Retrokids memory expansion. Did
you get it to plug in? If so, can you write a review and describe how
it works? (now back to 1977) The problem with the BPA is that here is
where the engineering stopped! When the Add-under got delayed Jay
Fenton was commisioned to come up with a "gap measure" and Bally
Basic 6002 was created. However the 300 baud taping interface must
have been a nightmare for them, as the origional engineering didn't
allow for it. It's a masterpiece of engineering to look at. Inside
there are 11 CMOS (higher dollar already in those days) circuit chips
that save current draw from the Arcade in such a way that it's a
wonder! Why you ask? Because the Arcades 5V regulator was
already "maxed out" except for the light pen, and COULDN'T take on
ANY more safely! You MAY be able to load it down with more and get
away with it, but: WHAT IS YOUR ARCADE WORTH TO YOU? If you start
putting an entire bunch of circuitry into the cartridge slot (or tie
it to the light pen jack, or both) you are taking a BIG risk! The
Bally engineers only allowed for the 300 baud interface with BB 6002
and NO MORE! Back in the 1980's if you "smoked" an Arcade you could
always go buy another, today one has to ask: WHAT IS YOUR ARCADE
REALLY WORTH TO YOU?
Unfortunatly, Multi-carts fall into this catagory as well because
they were NOT even imagined by the Bally engineers back in 1977. So,
let's look at some numbers of MAXIMUM ICC's, which are the upper
limits that these parts could draw on (and thereby endanger) the 5V
power source inside the Arcade. Note: If this power source fails the
remaining bias voltages CAN and WILL damage parts all over the
Arcade! The parts inside these Multi-carts (that are currently in
use) draw:

Ward shrake--M27C4001 4m EPROM 30.0ml---74LS32 4x2input or gate 9.8ml
8x-1-472 (or 8 4.7k resistors) 8.5ml

TOTAL for Multi-cart 48.3ml

CPUWIZ--M27C4001 4m EPROM 30.0ml 6 1k resistors 30.0ml

TOTAL for Multi-cart 60.0ml

Retrokids--2 M29F040CF 4m EEPROMs 15.0ml each (approx) ACT02 4x2input
nor gate less than 0.1mil (approx) 10x-1-472 4.7k resistor strip 8.5ml
note: I couldn't find "exact" matches of data sheets for nor gate or
EEPROM, but did find similar.

TOTAL for Multi-cart between 38.5 and 39.0 (approx)

Gambits--M27C801 8m EPROM 35.0ml 10A1-223G 0649 22k resistor strip
1.8ml 1N4148 or gate 0.0ml

TOTAL for Multi-cart 36.8ml

The real question now is exactly what was the current draw of the
origional 300 baud interface and old BB 6002 together, and what then
is the current draw of LiL' White Ram if you use it with ANY of these
Multi's. Well, the 300 Baud interface STAYS within 20.0ml (Ken
checked this for me when we were engineering LIL' White Ram). LIL'
White Ram uses about 8.5ml. That leaves finding the data sheet on:

CN9012N 7847 Y
S 72N620A02H1

This is the markings that I copied (as best as I could) from the 4kx8
PROM that is and always was inside my old Bally Basic 6002. However,
try as I might, I can't seem to locate a data sheet of any kind for
it. I think that it's probably a power hungry bugger, but until the
DC charactoristics chart turns up, I can't say for sure. However, a
look at what we do have should make someone who VALUES thier machine
hesitate. Ward made his Multi-cart BEFORE the schematic even appeared
on Bally Alley which means LIL' White Ram was NOT even considered
when it was being built (EB programs were figured to run with a Blue
Ram, Viper, or 64K R & L Ram Board which rely on thier own outside
power, same as the "Add Under" intended to have). The power drain
here was NOT figured into it! The power drain was DEFINATELY NOT a
consideration for CPUWIZ either. Gambits DID consider it, and
engineered acordingly. Retrokids didn't realize the importance of
this either, but "got lucky" by using the newer parts that were less
load on any system. If you do use a multi-cart often, (with or
without LIL' White Ram, or even a 300 baud interface) I obviously
suggest using Gambits Multi, or if not that, Retrokids until the
missing data sheet is located. Keep the others (for now) in your Zip
lock Freezer bag. After all, it's your Arcade and it's worth whatever
you think it's worth.

Now, did I miss something? If not, and there is no more input, and no
one wants to hear more clearification of the stuff that generated
discussion last time (or may do so this time) this "article" is 
considered complete.

Mike W

I agree with that.  There was a time when I didn't. I really only held onto the Astrocade.  I was sure that emulation was the way to go and that I could play any of those classic games on my PC.  Wrong.  It isn't until you know a piece of hardware very well that you realize that emulation just isn't going to replace what you had. really only held onto the Astrocade. I was sure that emulation was the way
to go and that I could play any of those classic games on my PC. Wrong. It
isn't until you know a piece of hardware very well that you realize that
emulation just isn't going to replace what you had. Some of the best known
systems emulation is probably as good as the real machine-- if you know
which emulator is best for which games and can overlook certain things

I'm not saying that it CAN'T happen, but I've never seen one of these third-party cartridges in a black case-- unless it was made by Mike White (but he used generic white labels).  If the original manufactures had run out of the grayish-colored cases back during the original manufacturing period, then perhaps they used black cases.  The black cases that are used are certainly third-party cases.  These are the same cases that Mike White has so many of.

The labels on the Ms. Candyman cartridge (item # 270233404372) looks legitimate-- and it would probably be very hard to fake that label (take a look at it to see what I mean).  The Treasure Trove label (item # 270233404355) also looks right-- but that would be a MUCH easier label to fake.

In summary, I haven't seen a black cartridge of either of those games, but that surely doesn't mean it isn't possible.

It's strange when we even have to ask these kinds of questions-- isn't it?

6226:
Glad you were able to load those MESS save-states for STWEEK, that's a
good way to save program listings, too.  Didn't know there needed to be
a sta[te] folder, but now I have one.  Sorry you had problems with the
spaces in the filenames.
Speaking of spaces, if you expand each space in "Mountain King" to where
the next token is at the start of the next line then it's much easier to
read - and only takes up 47 of the 48 lines.

Someone, somewhere said that "In the Hall of the ..." played forever,
but (as you can see from the code) it only keeps playing the same
twenty-six chords (and six of those are repeated), first with only one
channel turned on, then with one still muted, and then all three notes.
Then it repeats that cycle an octave higher, then higher still.  Lastly,
the whole process is repeated fifteen times.  The whole song takes about
seventeen minutes before stopping, although you do have to keep jiggling
the joystick occasionally to keep the screen from blanking.
I kept having to wait for the whole thing to finish because there is a
lock-out flag to stop someone from hitting ANALYZE again while it was
still analyzing, and the PLAY MUSIC is a part of that.  Even with MESS
un-throttled it only runs at double speed for me.

Using the keypad with or without an overlay is a pain - Let's see, I
need to print an "R" for Rest, that's a shifted "V" so first I'll hit
'cE' and then it's on the 'C' button.  Youch!  And there was no way to
tell if you were shifting or un-shifting until you entered a character.
Of course, that was back before you could pick up a 101-key keyboard
with a PS-2 connector for $2.00 new at the local flea-market.  If I do
load another song into this I'm going to just paste the ASCII straight
into an old *.sta file.

Actually saving the Music Score is another problem.  I was able to view
it with the View Memory window in the MESS debugger, to make sure it
matched the original from SONGS (except for the label addresses, of
course), but there is no provision to save it.
They must have been using a development machine (most likely CP/M at
that time), so it would have been much easier to just use the Music
Macros in a cross-assembler.  The result is still the same, and they
could have used the Note Names in the original SONGS source, too.

I was surprised at how fast it scanned through all 959 bytes in the
buffer, though, and resolved the labels without a second pass.  So,
KUDOS to Scot Norris if he wrote this Beta cartridge.  But, it probably
was only used as a DEMO, using music that was written elstwhere.

I wanted to make a 256-color display so I changed their horizontal
rows in the 66-color Rainbow Ver. 2 over to vertical columns (as can
be seen during the 2 second pause when starting) and doubled up on
the interrupts.  I also enabled their once-a-second routine so the
colors scroll like they were meant to, but the call to STIMER (System
Timer routine) that was in there interrupted the interrupts too much,
causing a nasty flicker, so I couldn't use that like I wanted to.
Since the Split Value always needed to be set to 5 anyway, I removed
that step and added some ghosted XOR text instead.  I ended up using
exactly the same amount of code as the earlier version - 390 bytes!

6243:
Ah-ha, that's clearer!  The candy-cane text was to differentiate it
from the "original".  The reason it's red & white is that you cannot
PLOP anything down without having the frame around it show up too.
You have to X-OR (or OR) it with what is already there, in this case
it was horizontal bars used to split each interrupt into two colors
(of odd and even, not the left/right dark and light split entered.)

Actually, the WHITE box next to the logo on Ver. 2 was caused by the
WRITP system routine leaving room to shift it over if it needed to,
and not part of the bitmap at all.  After inverting the bits of the
logo (to a negative of it) I wrote it IN white ON RED so it ended up
looking the same except for the overhanging part.
